preamble: The shift from the voiceless alveolar stop [t] to the alveolar fricative [s] is known as assibilation. It is frequently triggered by a following high-front vowel [i] or a palatal glide [j], where the stop gains friction and eventually loses its closure.

examples.note: Mazurzenie: Polish Masovian dialect assibilation where retroflex/palatal sibilants → alveolar; e.g., 'szary' [ʃaɾɨ] → [saɾɨ] (grey). Also shows t→ts in some forms.
Historical assibilation of t before i.
Assibilation of the dental stop before i + vowel.
Bantu spirantization: *t > s before the first-degree high vowel *i
Both stops spirantize; cf. Zulu impisi

sources: Lass, R. (1997). Historical Linguistics and Language Change. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511620928
